style: calm, natural hesitations, like explaining to a friend
slides: So, we know how to write every paragraph. Now, how do we put them together into an essay?
Look, there's no structure you have to write in.

Yes, you need an opening and a closing, and the body in the middle. But the body can be arranged in all kinds of ways. Mixed paragraphs, this before that. There's almost nothing you're not allowed to do.
But so you don't get mixed up, we recommend one structure. And if the content and the language you put into it are good, it can get the top score.
Now, a recommended structure has a few advantages.
One: it saves time. You don't have to think, for every essay: which structure fits here? Two arguments, or one? Rebuttal before or after? Should I split it?
And more than that, you have fixed connectors for every spot. The start of a paragraph, the middle, the weakening. Even fixed phrases, like 'Admittedly, there is some truth in this, but ...'.
Two: it has everything in the rubric. And your score depends on how well you meet each of the rubric's criteria.
Without a recommended structure, you might build an essay that misses part of it. For example:

no rebuttal paragraph. The raters expect you to deal with the other side, and a separate rebuttal paragraph is our way of doing that. Without it, your score goes down, even if your arguments are excellent.
Or, you decided to only reveal your position at the end of the essay. And these are just a few examples.
Three: writing in the recommended structure keeps you at the right length.
Someone who makes up their own structure might end up too short,
or get to fifty lines without finishing, because they wrote four argument paragraphs. Wait, what? I'm at line fifty, there's nowhere to write the closing, and I can't close the essay.
And maybe the thing I love most about the recommended structure... it simply prevents mistakes. It gives you boundaries.
You get a template. A real stencil. You pour the content in, and you move inside those boundaries.
I compare it to children's bowling. When kids play, so the ball doesn't fall into the gutter, they put up barriers on both sides.
When the ball drifts, it hits the barrier and comes back in. That's the recommended structure. Wherever you would have drifted out, it keeps you in the lane.
Maybe it won't be a strike in the end. But you'll knock down some pins, instead of an essay that misses completely.
So from this shape, we get the recommended structure. Opening and closing, same as before. And the body:
Argument one: why my side brings a benefit. Argument two: a second benefit, or the harm of the other side. Which is actually the same thing, because one side's harm is the other side's benefit.
Then I deal with an opposing view, and I weaken it with a third argument. A new one, not one I already used. Using one of those again would be repetition.
So everything is here. Dealing with the opposing view, arguments that are developed and explained, and a very clear main thread. Let's call it basic structure one.
Students often tell me: I tried, but my weakening in the rebuttal turned out to be argument two again. Is that okay?
No. That's repetition. Once you've used something in the essay, you don't use it again.
Think of the card game War. Everyone throws a card, and the highest card wins.
So I throw my first argument... an ace. Great, because I want my strongest argument first. It's the first time the rater sees my content. The opening didn't show any.
Then a king, or a queen. And when I get to the rebuttal, I have no good cards left. I can't pick up the ace and throw it again.
So what do I do? I just drop argument paragraph two, and I keep argument two for the rebuttal.
Because dealing with an opposing argument matters more to me than one more argument for my side.
And in the rebuttal, argument two does more. It supports my side, and it also weakens the opposing argument. Let's call it basic structure two.
By the way, with one paragraph less, you can make the opening and the argument paragraph richer. That's exactly when the longer opening, the rewrite one, is useful.
And again, if you write in this structure, with good content and language, it can get the top score. It's not like they give fewer points for it.
Here's a tip for anyone who has trouble finishing, or who's always just about out of time.
Start with argument one, and go straight to the rebuttal. Now you've already dealt with an opposing view.
Then, it depends on how much time is left. If you make it, add argument two. If not, skip it. You still have a complete essay, including the opposing view.
And that's better than argument one, argument two, and then no time for the rebuttal. Or a rushed weakening.
But wait, how do I know, when I write the opening, that I need the longer one? I start writing, argument one, argument two, and only at the end I find out I'm using the same argument again?
No. Before we start writing, we plan. Before the first word of the opening, I already know exactly what the essay will look like:
which paragraphs, and which argument goes in each paragraph. We do all that in the planning stage... the essay skeleton. That's the next lesson.
And one note. This structure is a tool, it's not an exam rule. What the raters do expect is that you deal with the other side, and this structure makes sure you do.
